subject: why does Lavaan converge normally with a purposefully underidentified model?

messages.author: a0ec8e0cf19a05fe
messages.subject: why does Lavaan converge normally with a purposefully underidentified model?
parts:
Hello.  In order to show students what happens when one fits a model that is underidentified, I generated data from a simple measurement model with one "latent" and four "observed" variables and then fit the model without fixing either the variance of the latent or any of the path coefficients.  I expected that lavaan would tell me that there were convergence problems or some other type of error message.  However, when I fit the model to the data, lavaan reports a normal convergence and even prints out a ML chi-square value and a null probability.  The only sign of a problem is that it can't calculate the SE of the parameters.  The degrees of freedom (1) show that neither the latent variance nor any of the path coefficients were fixed and the parTable() function (reproduced below) shows that all of the parameters were free.
Why (and how...) can lavaan converge and estimate values for these free parameters when the model is underidentified?  Why doesn't it print out a warning about underidentification?
Thanks for any help.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: why does Lavaan converge normally with a purposefully underidentified model?
parts:
On 12/05/2014 10:25 PM, Bill Shipley wrote:
> Why (and how...) can lavaan converge and estimate values for these free
> parameters when the model is underidentified? Why doesn't it print out
> a warning about underidentification?

Well, this seems not so strange to me.

Why do you still get estimates? Well, if a model is underidentified,
lavaan (or any other program for that matter) can usually still come up
with good estimates anyway (and some people exploit this 'feature'). The
solution, of course, may not be unique. If this is problematic, depends
on the setting.

Why 'convergence'? The optimizer has no idea if a model is identified or
not. It simply tries to minimize a discrepancy function. And it may very
well find a local minimum.

Why not a warning? Well, not getting standard errors is already a big
warning that something is wrong. Although this is not always due to
underidentification. Nevertheless, lavaan 0.5-17 does print:

"lavaan NOTE: this may be a symptom that the model is not identified"

The more interesting question is: can lavaan not detect this from just
scanning the parameter table? Perhaps, but it is not trivial. Just
following some rules of thumb is not enough. For example, for the
1-factor example, lavaan could check if either a factor loading was
fixed to a constant, or if the variance of the factor was fixed. But
suppose we use effect coding to fix the metric of the latent variable, as in

f =~ NA*x1 + a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3 + d*x4
f ~~ f # free
a + b + c + d == 4

we may falsely flag this model as underidentified. In short, determining
if a model is underidentified just by scanning the parameter table is
rather difficult.

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: why does Lavaan converge normally with a purposefully underidentified model?
parts:
> For the sake of a teaching example, you could run the model twice (both
> times underidentified) but with different starting values. That might
> lead to different solutions, which is what you'd want to demonstrate as
> the problem of underidentification.

In particular the starting value for the factor variance seems to have a
big impact, eg:


library(lavaan)
Data <- simulateData('f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4', sample.nobs = 1000)

model <- ' f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f ~~ start(0.1)*f
'

fit1 <- lavaan(model, auto.var = TRUE, data = Data)
summary(fit1)

model <- ' f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
f ~~ start(10)*f
'

fit2 <- lavaan(model, auto.var = TRUE, data = Data)
summary(fit2)

fitted(fit1)
fitted(fit2)


Yves.

parts:
Hello.  I wish to specify a model in which a latent variable is not measured by any observed variable but is a cause of observed variables.  For instance:
L--(5)-->o<--e
where L is a latent, o is an observed variable, and the path coefficient is fixed at 5.  I don't know how to specify this in lavaan.  It seems that lavaan requires that I have at least 1 observed indicator variable (i.e. L=~x) before I can add o~L.
I suspect that there is a way in lavaan to do this but can't figure it out.
On Wed, Dec 10, 2014 at 10:32 AM, Yves Rosseel <yros...@gmail.com> wrote:

For the sake of a teaching example, you could run the model twice (both
times underidentified) but with different starting values.  That might
lead to different solutions, which is what you'd want to demonstrate as
the problem of underidentification.

 In particular the starting value for the factor variance seems to have a big impact, eg:


library(lavaan)
Data <- simulateData('f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4', sample.nobs = 1000)

model <- ' f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
           f ~~ start(0.1)*f
         '

fit1 <- lavaan(model, auto.var = TRUE, data = Data)
summary(fit1)

model <- ' f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

         '

fit2 <- lavaan(model, auto.var = TRUE, data = Data)
summary(fit2)

fitted(fit1)
fitted(fit2)


Yves.

Bill--
     It is the same thing, whether you call the observed variable an indicator or measure, or not.  The distinction in behavior comes from indicators that load only on a single factor.  If this is true for your observed variable, then it is an indicator of the factor in every sense.
--Ed Rigdon
